body:
What is quantum computing?

Quantum computing is a method of processing information that uses the principles of quantum mechanics, the branch of physics that explains the behaviour of matter and energy at atomic and subatomic scales.

Ordinary computers process information using bits. Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits. The difference is not simply that a quantum computer uses a smaller or faster electronic component. A qubit can have quantum states and relationships that an ordinary bit cannot reproduce.

The most important concepts underlying quantum computing are qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum interference and measurement. These concepts explain how quantum information is represented, processed and converted into a readable result.

Classical bits: Information represented by 0 and 1

A bit is the smallest basic unit of information in classical computing. It has 2 possible values: 0 and 1.

In an electronic computer, these values are represented by distinguishable physical conditions, such as voltage levels. A bit may be represented by an electrical condition corresponding to 0 or another condition corresponding to 1.

For example, a conventional switch has 2 positions, on and off. This provides a useful analogy for binary information. Actual computer circuits use more sophisticated electronic devices, but they still encode and manipulate binary values.

Several bits can be combined to represent numbers, letters, images and instructions. For example, 2 classical bits can represent 4 combinations: 00, 01, 10 and 11. However, a particular 2-bit register contains only 1 of these combinations at a given instant.

What is a qubit?

A qubit, or quantum bit, is the basic unit of quantum information. It is a quantum system with 2 distinguishable basis states, conventionally called 0 and 1, that can also exist in a quantum superposition of those states.

The states 0 and 1 are the reference states used to describe and measure a qubit. They are often written as \(\lvert 0\rangle\) and \(\lvert 1\rangle\). The symbols identify quantum states; they do not mean that a qubit is an ordinary electrical switch.

Unlike a classical bit, a qubit can be prepared in a superposition involving both basis states. However, when it is measured in the standard computational basis, the result is still a single classical value: either 0 or 1.

Therefore, the essential difference is between the quantum state before measurement and the classical information obtained after measurement.

Physical systems that can act as qubits

Quantum information must be stored in a physical system. Suitable systems include certain states of atoms, ions, photons and specially designed electronic circuits.

  • Atomic or ionic qubits: 2 distinguishable quantum states of an atom or ion can represent the basis states.
  • Photonic qubits: Properties of individual photons, such as 2 chosen polarization states, can represent quantum information.
  • Superconducting qubits: Quantum states in specially designed superconducting electrical circuits can serve as qubits.

The common requirement is that the system can be prepared, manipulated and measured according to quantum-mechanical rules. Not every quantum computer uses the same physical technology.

The scientific foundation: Discrete quantum states

School-level atomic theory introduces the idea that electrons in atoms occupy permitted energy levels rather than arbitrary classical orbits. This is an example of quantization: certain physical quantities have distinct allowed values.

Quantum computing builds on the broader principles of quantum mechanics. A qubit uses 2 distinguishable quantum states as its computational basis. These states may be associated with energy, polarization or another suitable physical property.

The 2 states of a qubit need not be the electron shells shown in the elementary Bohr model of the atom. The atomic model provides a foundation for understanding discrete states, not a complete description of quantum-computer hardware.

Classical bits and qubits compared

FeatureClassical bitQubit
Basic unitBitQuantum bit
Possible information states0 or 1Basis states 0 and 1, or their superpositions
Standard readout0 or 10 or 1
Behaviour before measurementDefinite binary valueMay involve coherent quantum superposition
Relationships between unitsClassical correlationsClassical or quantum correlations, including entanglement

Why combining qubits is important

For 2 qubits, the computational basis contains 4 possible combinations: 00, 01, 10 and 11. A quantum state can be a superposition involving these combinations.

For 3 qubits, there are 8 basis combinations. More generally, a system of n qubits has 2n possible computational-basis combinations.

Classical registers of n bits also have 2n possible combinations. The difference is that a classical register has 1 definite combination at a time, whereas a quantum register can be prepared in a coherent superposition involving several combinations.

This does not mean that measuring 2 qubits provides all 4 combinations simultaneously. A standard measurement of the register produces only 1 of the possible 2-bit outcomes.

A qubit is not a classical bit that simply stores 0 and 1 as 2 readable answers. Its special feature is the ability to maintain a quantum superposition that can be manipulated before measurement.

Prelims focus

  • The basic unit of classical information is the bit.
  • The basic unit of quantum information is the qubit.
  • A qubit has 2 computational-basis states, conventionally 0 and 1.
  • Qubits can be implemented using atoms, ions, photons or superconducting circuits.
  • A standard measurement of 1 qubit gives either 0 or 1.
  • Trap: A qubit does not provide 2 readable classical values from a single measurement.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, 'Electricity and Circuits', printed pp. 116–121, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 4, 'Structure of the Atom', printed pp. 46–49, 2018–19 edition; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 'Quantum Computing Explained', sections on qubits and physical implementations, consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Quantum Mechanics Basics', sections on quantum states and measurement, consulted 5 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of quantum superposition

Quantum superposition is the principle that a quantum system can be in a state described by a coherent combination of different possible basis states.

For a qubit, the usual computational-basis states are 0 and 1. A qubit can be prepared in state 0, state 1 or a superposition involving both states.

The word coherent is important. It means that the components of the quantum state retain definite phase relationships that allow them to interfere. This makes a quantum superposition different from merely being uncertain whether an ordinary bit is 0 or 1.

How superposition affects measurement

Consider a qubit prepared in a balanced superposition of states 0 and 1. If it is measured in the computational basis, the outcomes have the following probabilities:

  • Probability of obtaining 0: 50%.
  • Probability of obtaining 1: 50%.

The measurement produces only 1 result. It does not produce a visible combination of 0 and 1.

If the same preparation and measurement are repeated many times, approximately half the measurements are expected to produce 0 and half to produce 1. This distribution becomes more evident over many trials; an individual trial cannot reveal the full probability distribution.

A balanced superposition is only 1 example. Other superpositions can give unequal measurement probabilities, such as 80% for 0 and 20% for 1. Therefore, superposition does not necessarily mean a 50:50 probability distribution.

What happens after measurement?

When a qubit is measured in the computational basis, the result is 0 or 1. In the standard description of projective measurement, the state after measurement becomes the corresponding measured basis state.

For example, if the result is 0, an immediate repeated measurement in the same basis, with no intervening operation, gives 0 again.

The original superposition is not available for further coherent processing after that measurement. This is why quantum computations normally manipulate the quantum state before obtaining their final classical result.

Measurement is not the same as reading an ordinary stored bit. Measurement of a superposed qubit generally produces a probabilistic outcome and changes the state being measured.

Superposition is not ordinary uncertainty

Suppose an ordinary computer randomly selects 0 or 1 with equal probability. Before looking at the result, an observer may not know which value was chosen. However, the classical bit already has a definite value.

Now consider a qubit prepared in a balanced superposition. Measuring it may also produce 0 or 1 with equal probability. Nevertheless, the unmeasured quantum state is not equivalent to the ordinary random bit.

The difference becomes apparent when further operations are applied before measurement. The components of a coherent quantum superposition can interfere with one another. An ordinary statistical mixture of classical values does not have the same quantum interference behaviour.

Quantum interference

Quantum interference occurs when components of quantum states combine so that some possible outcomes are reinforced and others are weakened or cancelled.

Interference is related to the wave-like behaviour of quantum systems. Ordinary waves provide a familiar analogy:

  • Constructive interference: When suitable wave components combine, they reinforce one another.
  • Destructive interference: When suitable wave components combine oppositely, they weaken or cancel one another.

In quantum computing, carefully chosen operations change the relative phases and amplitudes of quantum-state components. As a result, later measurement probabilities can become larger for some outcomes and smaller for others.

The relevant phase relationships are not visible from the initial measurement probabilities alone. Consequently, 2 different quantum preparations can have the same immediate measurement probabilities but respond differently to later operations.

Why interference matters in quantum computing

Creating a superposition does not automatically solve a problem. An algorithm must manipulate the quantum state so that the final measurement is likely to produce a useful result.

Quantum interference is one of the main ways that quantum algorithms achieve this. The aim is to increase the probability of obtaining useful outcomes while reducing the probability of obtaining unsuitable ones.

This is why a quantum computer is not simply a machine that tries every possible answer and displays them all. Its usefulness depends on how quantum operations shape the probability distribution before measurement.

Superposition and uncertainty

A superposition is a precise quantum-mechanical description, not merely a statement that an observer lacks information. Quantum theory predicts the probabilities of measurement outcomes using the state and the measurement being performed.

Which measurement is chosen matters. The familiar outcomes 0 and 1 refer to measurement in the computational basis. A different measurement basis can produce a different set of outcome probabilities for the same initially prepared state.

For introductory quantum computing, the central point is that the quantum state can be manipulated coherently before it is measured and converted into an ordinary classical result.

Prelims focus

  • Superposition is a coherent combination of quantum basis states.
  • A balanced superposition of 0 and 1 gives 50% probability for each outcome in the computational basis.
  • Superpositions do not always have equal measurement probabilities.
  • A single computational-basis measurement produces either 0 or 1.
  • Quantum interference can reinforce or suppress possible measurement outcomes.
  • Trap: A classical random bit and a coherent qubit superposition are not physically equivalent, even when their immediate measurement statistics are the same.

[Sources: IBM Quantum Learning, 'Quantum Mechanics Basics', sections 'Quantum State Representation', 'Measurements' and 'Measurement in Different Bases', consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Superposition with Qiskit', section on superposition and phase coherence, consulted 5 November 2026; IBM Quantum Learning, 'Basics of Quantum Information', 'Single Systems: Quantum Information', section 'Measuring Quantum States', consulted 5 November 2026.]
